text: dsh-limit-break 为 DSH 注册跨会话记忆和网页抓取工具。它把事实存入本地 JSON，支持保存、关键词检索和存储统计；抓取时依次尝试普通请求、IPv6、IPv4及适用的 Wikipedia API 地址，并记住成功路线。适合希望在新会话找回事实或在请求失败时继续获取网页内容的用户。无需 API 密钥；备用 IP 路线默认使用 curl。

dsh-limit-break adds cross-session memory and resilient fetching to DSH. Tools save facts in local JSON, search them later, and report store statistics. Fetch retries direct, IPv6, IPv4, or applicable Wikipedia API routes, remembering success. No API key is needed; IP fallback uses curl.
希望 DSH 新会话还能查到以前保存的重要事实。
普通网页请求超时或连接重置时，有没有办法换路线再试？
Can I save useful facts now and look them up in a later DSH session?
dsh-limit-break 的功能「跨会话事实记忆」：通过 memory_save 保存或更新带稳定 ID 的事实，存入本地 JSON；新会话可用 memory_recall 按关键词排序检索，或按 ID 精确读取。
dsh-limit-break 的功能「多路线网页抓取」：调用 resilient_fetch 并提供 HTTP(S) URL；它按可用路线重试请求，并返回响应内容、状态及成功路线，成功的备用路线会供后续请求优先使用。
dsh-limit-break 会向用户提供的 URL 发出请求；适用的 Wikipedia 页面会改用 api.wikimedia.org。（见 lib/index.js:414-422、710-766）

dsh-limit-break README · dsh-limit-break：Four small tools for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) that came out of a
self-benchmark: two things an agent is normally told it cannot do, made cheap enough to just do.

dsh-limit-break README · dsh-limit-break：| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `memory_recall` | Ranked search over a JSON fact store that outlives the session. Omit `query` to list everything. |
| `memory_save` | Write or overwrite one fact: `{ id, statement, value?, unit?, details?, tags?, source? }`. |
| `resilient_fetch` | Fetch with a four-rung ladder and a report of which rung answered. |
| `memory_stats` | Where the store is, how many facts, how big. |

dsh-limit-break README · dsh-limit-break：Zero npm dependencies. No import-time side effects. Everything fails soft — a broken store or a dead
network returns an error object, never an exception that could take the host down.

dsh-limit-break README · dsh-limit-break：**Recall quality.** `memory_recall` is measured, not vibed: `tools/recall-bench.mjs` runs 20
hand-labelled questions against the live store and prints hit@1 / hit@3 / MRR. At 1.5.0 the ranking
skips English stopwords, stems, matches whole words (with a prefix fallback, so `ray` finds
`raytracer`), splits dotted ids into segments, weights each query token by inverse document
frequency, and rewards a whole-phrase hit: **hit@1 0.75 → 0.95, MRR 0.867 → 0.975** on the same 20
questions and the same 20 facts. The one remaining miss is a genuinely ambiguous question that
matches two benchmark facts.

dsh-limit-break README · dsh-limit-break：**Runtime requirement: `curl`.** Rung 1 of the fetch ladder is plain `fetch` and needs nothing; rungs
2–4 (IPv6 → IPv4 → sibling hostname) shell out to `curl`, so it has to be on `PATH`. Windows 10+,
macOS and mainstream Linux all ship it. Without it the ladder degrades to rung 1 and says so in the
report instead of pretending it climbed.

dsh-limit-break README · Why these four：**Memory.** A session starts from zero. A store on disk plus a read at the start is enough to beat
that. Measured with two brand-new agents, zero context, the same five questions: **5/5 with the
store, 0/5 without** — and the control did not hallucinate, it answered "I don't have that" five
times.

dsh-limit-break README · Why these four：**Network.** The reflex "this host is unreachable" is wrong more often than it is right. Measured on
one network, same edge IP, 75 seconds apart: `api.wikimedia.org` → 200 in 0.43 s,
`en.wikipedia.org` → connection reset in 1.21 s, `api.wikimedia.org` again → 200 in 0.39 s. The
block was keyed on the TLS hostname, not the address. So the ladder tries, in order: plain fetch →
IPv6 → IPv4 → a **sibling hostname of the same service** whose certificate still verifies
(`*/wiki/Title` → `api.wikimedia.org/core/v1/wikipedia/<lang>/page/<Title>`).

dsh-limit-break README · Why these four：It does **not** disable certificate verification and does not route through a proxy that would
impersonate the origin. Those are MITM, not workarounds.

dsh-limit-break README · Why these four：**The ladder learns.** A fallback rung that worked is written back as `network.route.<host>` and the
next call to that host starts there; if a plain fetch starts working again the route is deleted (host
self-heals). Measured on `en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method`, 12 s per-rung timeout: cold
**12.1 s** (rung 1 burned the timeout, rung 4 answered) → warm **1.08 s / 1.14 s**, one attempt
instead of two — **11.2× faster**. Numbers come from `tools/fetch-route-bench.mjs`.

dsh-limit-break README · Install：```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-limit-break
```

Then restart that profile. In the desktop app, install it from **Settings → Plugins** instead — the
desktop profile is owned by the app's plugin manager.

The package declares `dsh.bundle` and ships `cordis.patch.yml`, so `dsh plugin add` mounts it with no
manual editing. If you are mounting it by hand, add to `profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: limit-break
      name: dsh-limit-break
```

dsh-limit-break README · Install：A hand-mounted entry still needs the package on the profile's dependency list — a bare `insert` for a
package the profile does not declare is silently ignored.

dsh-limit-break README · The store：`$DSH_HOME/memory/facts.json`, schema:

```json
{ "schema_version": 1,
  "facts": [ { "id": "", "topic": "", "statement": "", "value": "", "unit": "",
               "details": "", "source": "", "timestamp": "", "tags": [] } ] }
```

dsh-limit-break README · The store：Plain JSON on purpose: anything that can read a file can use it, with or without this plugin.
Writes are tmp-file + rename, and a save takes a `.facts.lock` (created `O_EXCL`, stolen after
15 s if its writer died) around the whole read-modify-write, so two sessions saving at the same
moment both keep their facts. `tools/concurrency-selftest.mjs` states the numbers: 16–17 of 48
saves lost before the lock, 0 after.

dsh-limit-break README · Disable / remove：* Hot: set `disabled: true` on the entry in `cordis.patch.yml` — Cordis recomposes in about a second.
* Cold: `dsh plugin remove dsh-limit-break`, then restart.
* The store is not deleted by either. It lives in `$DSH_HOME/memory/` and is safe to keep.

dsh-limit-break README · Known limits：* **Tools are visible only to sessions opened after the mount.** A session created before the
  plugin mounted keeps its tool snapshot; new tools do not appear until a new session. Not fixable
  from the plugin side (the tool list is materialised per session).
* **Concurrent saves serialise, and wait at most 8 s.** A second session saving at the same moment
  waits for the lock instead of losing its fact; if the holder is wedged, the save returns
  `{ ok: false, code: "memory.locked" }` rather than hanging. Read paths take no lock, so a save
  still cannot stop a reader from seeing the previous snapshot.
* **The fetch ladder is hostname-level.** It does not defeat IP-level blocks, TLS interception,
  or a proxy that terminates the connection; it does not skip certificate verification.
* **A remembered route is a bet with a 14-day expiry.** The ladder trusts `network.route.<host>` for
  two weeks and drops it as soon as a direct request works; if the winning rung starts failing the
  call still walks the rest of the ladder, it just pays that one rung first.

dsh-limit-break README · Privacy：Nothing leaves the machine. `resilient_fetch` makes the request you asked for; the memory tools read
and write one local file.
